newsitem.title: UK: Gas storage becomes key as UK competition hots up.
newsitem.headline: Gas storage becomes key as UK competition hots up.

text.p: Gas storage will become a vital tool for dealing with huge swings in demand from household gas consumers and limiting price volatility as Britain's new suppliers move into the domestic sector, industry watchers said.
At times of peak winter demand, suppliers' reserves of North Sea gas at the beach and in storage can be exhausted, forcing them to bid up prices in the spot market.
"Every player in the domestic sector needs to look at the way it covers peak demand," said Julian Kennedy of Edinburgh-based consultants Wood Mackenzie.

Gas demand in the U.K. domestic sector swings by 200 to 300 percent according to the weather. While industrial and commercial demand also fluctuates, suppliers have other means of coping with peak demand such as interruptible contracts, Kennedy said.

London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), which recently launched a natural gas futures contract, believes that a lack of storage in the U.K. could be a key driver of price volatility as the gas market opens up to further competition.
Gas storage capacity in the United States is equivalent to 20 percent of annual consumption, but British storage meets only five percent of yearly demand, the IPE said.

And an annual tendering process for booking storage capacity -- which at present is controlled exclusively by BG plc's pipeline and storage arm TransCo -- gives gas suppliers little room for manoeuvre.
"It means that they have to take a fairly detailed view of supply and demand early in the year," said Wood Mackenzie's Kennedy.
This year's tender opened last week ready for allocation of capacity by May 1, the start of the storage year, said Irene Davies, commercial storage executive at TransCo.
"Customers fill up in the summer and empty in the winter," she said.
Low spot prices this winter, which fell below the critical 10 pence a therm level in mid-February, were partly the result of summer hoarding, said Kennedy.

"Low prices on the market can be traced back to the summer when players were covering their Jan/Feb positions," he said. "(This winter) turned out to be milder on the whole than last year and people have had to unwind their positions."

To gain more storage flexibility, independent gas supplier United Gas, a subsidiary of U.S. Utilicorp United Inc, is already developing its own capacity in salt cavities in Cheshire, and industry analysts believe that other independents will soon follow suit.
United Gas will be able to move gas from its 11.3 million cubic metre storage into the transmission system in "less than an hour". The company expects the storage to be in use by late 1999.

TransCo's main storage facility is Rough, a mostly-depleted gas field 29 kilometres off the Yorkshire coast. The field holds 2.8 billion cubic metres of gas, or 82 percent of the company's storage capacity. Gas from Rough is landed at the Easington terminal in North Humberside on Britain's east coast.
Gas is stored onshore by TransCo in salt cavities at Hornsea in East Yorkshire, which holds 189 million cubic metres of gas and is linked directly to the National Transmission System (NTS).
Salt cavities at Seal Sands on Teesside can store 1.83 million cubic metres of gas at high pressure.
TransCo also stores gas as liquefied natural gas (LNG) at five strategic sites around Britain, with a total capacity of 20,000 tonnes.
LNG takes up only 1/600 of the volume of dry gas and is used by TransCo to meet extreme peak demand in cold weather.
